parts:
I am trying to fit a relatively simple hierarchical random effects Poisson count model.  I have setup the following model and it seems to run OK, but my parameters(b) are distributed as independent normals.  My code is below:

data {
    int<lower=1> n;         // number of obs
    int<lower=1> J;         // number of Rs
    int<lower=1> L;         // # of vars
    int<lower=1> id[n];     // Group ID (1, 2, 3, ..., nobs)  Must be sequenced 1,2,3,...
    int<lower=0> y[n];      // estimated counts (1 per obs)
    matrix[n,L] x;          // x matrix including intercept
}

parameters {
    matrix[J,L] b;          // matrix of parameters
}

transformed parameters {

}

model {

    real eta[n];

  // Priors
    for (l in 1:L) {
        for (j in 1:J) {
            b[j,l] ~ normal(0, 100);
        }
    }


  // LLike
    for (i in 1:n) {
      eta[i] <- exp(b[id[i],1] .* x[i,1] + b[id[i],2] .* x[i,2] +
                b[id[i],3] .* x[i,3]);
      y[i] ~ poisson(eta[i]);
    }

}

1) How should I change this to have multivariate normal parameters (b's)?
2) Is there any way I can vectorize this simple example so I can learn how to write better code?

I apologize if these are such simple questions and would accept any references to examples in the documentation or elsewhere.  What I am trying to build up to is a hierarchical model with varying slopes and group-level predictors of those slopes, but I also want to model the correlation among the slopes.  So I am trying to build the model in steps.  The example I am thinking of is chapter 17 of Gelman & Hill's text.

Thank you

On Thursday, March 28, 2013 7:57:18 PM UTC-4, Tom Eagle wrote:
1) How should I change this to have multivariate normal parameters (b's)?
If you intend to have a diagonal covariance matrix, it is best to use (a product of) univariate normals.
2) Is there any way I can vectorize this simple example so I can learn how to write better code?
Here is how I would do it:

data {
   int<lower=1> n;         // number of obs
   int<lower=1> J;         // number of Rs
   int<lower=1> L;         // # of vars
   int<lower=1> id[n];     // Group ID (1, 2, 3, ..., nobs)  Must be sequenced 1,2,3,...
   int<lower=0> y[n];      // estimated counts (1 per obs)
   matrix[n,L] x;          // x matrix including intercept
}

parameters {

vector[L] b[J];          // array of vectors
}

model {
   real log_eta[n];
   int id_i;

   // Priors
for (j in 1:J) {

b[j] ~ normal(0, 100);
   }

   // linear predictor
for (i in 1:n) {

id_i <- id[i]  
     log_eta[i] <- b[id_i,1] * x[i,1] // if x[i,1] is always 1, don't multiply
                   + b[id_i,2] * x[i,2] + b[id_i,3] * x[i,3];
   }
   y ~ poisson_log(log_eta); // log-likelihood
}

On Thursday, March 28, 2013 8:50:33 PM UTC-4, Tom Eagle wrote: 
However, I would like the b's to be correlated, not have a diagonal covariance matrix.  How might I set that up?

If you have a prior covariance matrix, you can just use the syntax in the manual for multi_normal:

coefficients ~ multi_normal(zeros, Sigma);

It is faster to use a precision matrix (the inverse of a covariance matrix), in which case you could do

coefficients ~ multi_normal_prec(zeros, Sigma);

where Sigma is the precision matrix. If you want to use the same covariance matrix or precision matrix for a bunch of coefficient vectors, it can be more efficient to do the multi_normal part manually by incrementing lp__.

Ben

There's a simple explanation: ineffective error handling on
our part. We're working on catching all the exceptions and
indexing errors that might induce segfaults on the R side.
It's not such a huge issue from the command-line with a single
chain, but it's far better for us to spit out an informative
error message. From R, it's terribly rude of RStan to kill
the whole R process. (Makes me think of a bratty kid upsetting
a game of checkers because he's losing.)

Ben -- do you know what's causing the error in the code?
I'm going to go do some checks in all of our blocks for
indexing errors leaking out. And for var instantiations. I
thought we'd gotten them all, but this is still the most
likely cause of segfaults.

- Bob
